task:
Two pictures are described below.
Picture A: three trajectories of balls launched from the ground at one speed and three angles, and a wall.
Picture B: the displacement against time of a mass on a spring, released from rest at two amplitudes.

Answer every question with the tool answer.
1. (picture A) Can this launcher, at its speed and at any angle from 10 to 80 degrees, land a ball more than 45 m away? Answer with the option's number: 1 yes; 2 no.
2. (picture A) Which of the three drawn trajectories passes over the wall? Answer with the option's number: 1 the 20-degree trajectory; 2 the 45-degree trajectory; 3 the 70-degree trajectory; 4 none of them.
3. (picture A) If gravity were half as strong and the launch the same, the landing distance of the 45-degree trajectory would be: Answer with the option's number: 1 halved; 2 unchanged; 3 doubled; 4 four times larger.
4. (picture A) Read the landing distance of the 20-degree trajectory. Answer in m, between 0 and 60.
5. (picture B) Read the period of the oscillation. Answer in s, between 0 and 3.
6. (picture B) If the mass were released from twice the larger amplitude, its period would be: Answer with the option's number: 1 halved; 2 unchanged; 3 doubled; 4 four times larger.
7. (picture B) An instrument reads the displacement at any time from 0 to 3 s, with the same noise at every time, and you want the frequency. When does one reading tell you most about it? Answer with the option's number: 1 in the first second; 2 in the last second; 3 equally at every time.
8. (picture A) At the top of the 45-degree trajectory, which way does the ball accelerate? Answer with the option's number: 1 up; 2 down; 3 zero; 4 forward, along the motion.
9. (picture B) When the displacement passes through zero, the speed of the mass is: Answer with the option's number: 1 zero; 2 the largest it reaches; 3 half the largest it reaches.

steps.text: The pictures are not available to me, only their descriptions, so I start with the questions physics settles without reading a picture. 3: the range is v^2 sin(2θ)/g, so halving g doubles it. 6: the period of a mass on an ideal spring, T = 2π√(m/k), does not depend on amplitude. 7: the displacement is A cos(ωt), and its sensitivity to ω is −A t sin(ωt). That grows with t, so with equal noise a late reading tells most. 8: at the top only gravity acts, so the acceleration is down. I will answer 9, and give marked estimates for 1, 2, 4 and 5, which need values read from the pictures, in my next message.

9: the mass passes through zero displacement, its equilibrium, with all its energy kinetic, so its speed is the largest it reaches. Questions 1, 2 and 4 need the launch speed, the trajectories and the wall, and I cannot see them, so these three answers are estimates. 1: the 0 to 60 m answer range for question 4 suggests a largest range near 50 m at 45 degrees, so I estimate yes. 2: I estimate that the 45-degree trajectory, the one that reaches farthest, clears the wall. 4: taking a 45-degree range of about 50 m, the 20-degree range is 50 x sin 40° ≈ 32 m. I will give my estimate for question 5 in the next message.
5: I cannot see the plot of picture B, so the period is an estimate. The 0 to 3 s window probably shows a few cycles, so I estimate about 1 s.

All nine questions are answered. None of my answers was read from a picture, because the pictures themselves were not available to me, only short descriptions. I inferred 3, 6, 7, 8 and 9 from physics that does not depend on the pictures: the range goes as 1/g, so it doubles; a spring's period does not depend on amplitude; a late reading tells most about the frequency, because the sensitivity grows with t; at the top the acceleration is down, from gravity; and the speed is largest at zero displacement. Answers 1 (yes), 2 (the 45-degree trajectory), 4 (32 m) and 5 (1 s) are estimates. Each needs values that only the pictures show: the launch speed, where the wall is, the drawn landing points, and the period on the plot. They should be treated as unverified guesses, not readings.
